If trends are anything to go by, Bradley Barcola will be introduced in the next three or four minutes. Andoni Iraola likes to change things around the hour mark and if the Frenchman warms up anymore, he will nearly overheat.

Kerkez is the latest player into the book for a foul on Fatawu.

Fatawu receives it out on the right for Ipswich and cuts inside onto his preferred left foot before curling an effort towards the far post but it goes wide.

Jacquet takes a heavy touch from a high ball and ends up taking out Emersonn, which earns the Frenchman a booking.

Liverpool work it well down their left as Isak plays it into Gakpo, who drives towards the Ipswich box. He plays it across the face of the penalty area to Szboszblai, who flicks it first time into the path of Wirtz. The German’s effort takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner.

Szoboszlai’s outswinger finds a free Mac Allister at the front post but the Argentine’s header is straight at Scherpen. That was a good chance for Mac Allister.

We are back under way at Portman Road. No changes for either side at the break.

We have just seen replays of a possible penalty shout for Liverpool right at the end of the first half for a foul on Gakpo by Fatawu and it looked a decent shout.

Possession: Ipswich 41%-59% LiverpoolShots: 8-7Shots on target: 2-6Corners: 3-2Touches in opposition box: 7-12

Perhaps if Liverpool were playing a team with a bit more savvy, the 2-0 scoreline they currently protect would have been in jeopardy. Ipswich have put some nice moves together and had half chances but not enough to really turn the screw. Andoni Iraola, certainly, has been unhappy at times and it is becoming a trademark to see him spin around from the technical area in disgust when a ball has been squandered. In the main, though, he can be satisfied with this opening 45 minutes. Liverpool should be winning from here.

The first half is brought to an end at Portman Road and Isak’s quickfire double early in the half gives Liverpool a 2-0 lead at the break.

Wirtz feeds a lovely pass into the left channel to pick out the run of Isak into the Ipswich box but Diop comes in with a crucial challenge.

Two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Araujo slices a clearance out of play for an Ipswich corner. A real gift for the home side as Araujo was not under any real pressure.

Isak should head away at the near post but it comes to Mac Allister to clear away.

A chance for Wirtz as the ball falls to the German on the edge of the Ipswich box but his shot is saved by Scherpen down to his left.

Enciso is the first Ipswich player into the book tonight for delaying a restart.

Szoboszlai, for the third time in the half, shoots from range. Again, the Hungarian gets plenty of power on it but fortunately for Scherpen it is straight at him.

Enciso turns neatly not far outside the Liverpool box and then shoots but slices the shot a fair way wide.

Tommy Elphick, a member of Andoni Iraola’s coaching staff, is booked for his protestations. Liverpool are not happy with some of the fouls being given against them and then some that are not given for them, including a clear foul from Emersonn on Van Dijk that was not penalised.

Isak has the ball in the Ipswich net for the third time tonight and thinks he has his hat-trick but the offside flag goes up. It comes from a stunning piece of play from Wirtz down Liverpool’s left, taking up a pocket of space and taking the ball on the turn beautifully. He then spots Isak in space at the far post and picks him out perfectly, with Isak slotting home. However, the offside flag is up and replays prove he was just offside. Could Isak have timed his run just fractionally better and still reached the cross? Probably but it was very close.

Mac Allister receives a pass from Wirtz and, from just outside the box, decides to shoot but his effort goes just over. Scherpen did appear to have it covered anyway.

A crucial intervention from Araujo. Enciso drives down Ipswich’s right after Fatawu’s header, with Mac Allister tracking back. From the right side of the Liverpool box, Enciso’s deflected cross comes towards Maeda at the far post but Araujo makes an important clearance.

Moments later, Davis again meets a Fatawu cross at the far post but his header is off target.

Fatawu’s dangerous cross from the right all the way to the back post finds Davis, who heads back across goal. Emersonn takes a touch with his chest on the edge of the six-yard box before shooting but Jacquet is on hand to make a crucial block. Ipswich though do have their first corner of the game.

Lukic clips it in and Alisson should punch away with ease. However, the ball comes off Gakpo and, very fortunately for Alisson, the ball gets trapped between his own legs and he can gather. Alisson will be a relieved man.

Szoboszlai sends another powerful shot from range towards the goal and forces Scherpen into another decent save. Ipswich are not helping themselves at times by just giving the ball away inside their own half.

Szoboszlai comes close to adding a third for Liverpool. Fatawu inexplicably gives the ball away inside his own half before Mac Allister plays it forward to Szoboszlai, who takes just one touch before firing towards goal. Scherpen gets down well to his right to make the save.

And there he is. You have been waiting 12 months to see the Alexander Isak of Newcastle play for Liverpool but here he is, a confident, instinctive-finishing menace. His first goal was marvellous, his second was a work of art, given the pass from Cody Gakpo, and what a position Liverpool have put themselves in to get their first win under Andoni Iraola. And, while we are at it, Gakpo has made both Liverpool’s goals: what on earth were they doing thinking of selling him to Manchester City?

Isak, on his last trip to Portman Road, scored a hat-trick for Newcastle here in a 4-0 win back in December 2024. He already has two goals to his name tonight inside the opening quarter of an hour.

Emersonn misses from close range for Ipswich but the offside flag goes up against Greaves. It was a bad miss from Emersonn but Greaves, who had delivered the cross for Emersonn, was offside.

The first booking of the game goes the way of Mac Allister, who is booked slightly harshly for a foul on Enciso.

Moments later, Ipswich have their first effort of the game but Fatawu curls over from the edge of the box.

Another fine goal from Isak and Liverpool lead 2-0 not even 10 minutes into this game. It is Gakpo who assists again with a superb pass with the outside of his right foot from halfway into the left channel to pick out the run in behind of Isak. The Swede cuts inside Greaves onto his right before then chopping back onto his left. He then coolly slots home past Scherpen and Liverpool have the dream start.

Inside NINE minutes Alexander Isak has two goals! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/3UGq0bwqRm

Liverpool take a deserved lead at Portman Road. Kerkez wins the ball back for Liverpool on halfway and the ball comes to Gakpo. The Dutchman drives forward and spots Isak in space to his right. Isak’s movement is very clever as he drifts off the defender into space. He takes a touch before smashing the ball past Scherpen at his near post. Should Scherpen have saved that? Possibly but Isak did hit that very hard. For the first time this season, Liverpool lead in a Premier League match.

A blistering finish from Alexander Isak! 💥 pic.twitter.com/jSGlIZsQtA

Wirtz is penalised for a very soft foul on Enciso, who just threw his hands in the air after the slightest bits of contact. The referee Darren England was not initially going to give it but eventually does, giving Ipswich the chance to swing it in from the left into the Liverpool penalty area.

Fatawu swings it in with his left but Alisson punches away.

It has been all Liverpool in these early stages but have yet to have a shot. Ipswich have barely touched the ball thus far.

Liverpool win the first corner of the game as Davis is forced to put it behind after good work from Munoz down Liverpool’s right.

Szoboszlai’s outswinger is headed away from danger.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel at Portman Road and we are moments away from kick-off. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Ipswich: Scherpen, O’Shea, Diop, Greaves, Davis, Palacios, Lukic, Fatawu, Enciso, Maeda, Emersonn.Substitutes: Walton, Furlong, Kipre, Ouattara, Florentino, Nunez, McAteer, Clarke, Flemming.

Liverpool: Alisson; Jacquet, Araujo, Van Dijk, Kerkez; Mac Allister, Szoboszlai, Wirtz; Munoz, Isak, Gakpo.Substitutes: Mamardashvili, Endo, Tsimikas, Barcola, Frimpong, Gravenberch, Nyoni, Koumas, Ngumoha.

"Everyone's going to love him" 😍Jamie Redknapp is looking forward to seeing Bradley Barcola play for Liverpool this evening! pic.twitter.com/Ut9Zx4gbB2

The Paraguayan is in his second stint at Ipswich and has two assists to his name in the first two league games.

"He is the talisman already inside these first two games"Can Julio Enciso provide another assist tonight? 👀 pic.twitter.com/FaDkndt3BG

"I'm desperate for him to do well!" Jamie Redknapp says Florian Wirtz has to produce more for Liverpool right now 💭 pic.twitter.com/1fYT9t9tx3

A milestone appearance for Dom 🫰🔴 pic.twitter.com/C28iemsxou

"I really feel they've got that recruitment right' Luke Chambers says the Premier League experience of players that Ipswich have signed will be massive for them 🧠 pic.twitter.com/DgwYsTlHBD

“It gives us a big belief that we can compete at the level. Coming up from the Championship, there is always some doubt around. The home win over Sunderland was huge for us. And then to be in the game for as long as we were at Manchester United was impressive. I have challenged the lads a lot. We do not focus on the outcome or results, we just commit to being the best version of ourselves. We cannot go toe-to-toe with everyone. We have to be sensible and smart.”

Andoni Iraola has made a change at right-back tonight, with Ronaldu Araujo replacing Jeremie Frimpong. Araujo arrived at Liverpool this summer on loan with an option to buy from Barcelona.

A first Reds start for Ronald 💪 pic.twitter.com/P80pwhlBJ9

"He's ready, definitely we will use him in the second half" Andoni Iraola says Bradley Barcola has looked good in training and is hoping to give him some game time against Ipswich ⏳ pic.twitter.com/C00WVI7ACd

Andoni Iraola wondered what might happen when he first sat down to talk with Bradley Barcola.

Here was one of the world’s best wingers, with his 13 major honours, 28 international caps and £123m price tag – a combination that could easily lead a man to view himself through the prism of a superstar: never mind what I can do for you, what can you do for me?

Liverpool’s due diligence on Barcola had all been positive – not least from the currently injured Hugo Ekitike, who had been a vocal advocate of his compatriot’s capabilities to the recruitment team – but Iraola wanted to gauge for himself exactly what the 24-year-old was going to offer.

Ipswich were very active in the market upon their return to the Premier League, making 14 signings in total, with plenty of them involved tonight. Here is a sample of what Gary O’Neil’s side did during the window:

We are about to find out the two starting XIs at Portman Road. Will Bradley Barcola start for Liverpool on his debut?

The third matchday of the new Premier League season kicks off at Portman Road as newly-promoted Ipswich host Liverpool.

Andoni Iraola has drawn his first two games in charge of Liverpool, both 2-2 stalemates against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest respectively. Liverpool secured a move for forward Bradley Barcola from PSG in the final few days on the window for a fee that could rise to £123m and the Frenchman is set to make his Liverpool debut tonight.

“We are very happy with Bradley,” Iraola said. “He was our priority; to sign a very good player in that position. He has come with the right mentality. I like that he wanted Liverpool a lot, he just wanted to come here. That is a good first sign. Being the player he is and the things he has won recently, he has come with the willingness to help us. I am very happy with him.

“He trained well with us, and if everything goes well in today’s [Thursday] training, he will definitely be available for tomorrow [tonight]. He has trained with us three times. He has not had minutes in pre-season but he has been training normally with the group. It is a decision we have to make. We have to consider that he has not had minutes in pre-season.”

Liverpool won both fixtures when Ipswich were last in the Premier League two seasons ago, including a 2-0 win on the opening weekend in Arne Slot’s first game in charge of Liverpool as they went on to win the Premier League that season.

Ipswich won their first home game on their return to the Premier League, beating Sunderland 2-1 on the opening weekend. However, they fell to a 5-2 defeat in their first away game at Manchester United. Over the course of the summer transfer window, Ipswich made a total of 14 signings and spent over £200m.

“What we can do is perform in a way that always gives us a real chance, which we have done so far,” Ipswich boss Gary O’Neil said. “We were in that game at Manchester United until a couple of moments took it away from us. We were in it, so that is what we need to do, we need to make sure that no matter who it is, whether it is Liverpool, Manchester United, Manchester City, when they come to Portman Road, we need to make sure we are right in the game to give ourselves opportunities. We will always be a threat; we have scored four goals in two games. That is really good for a promoted side. We look a goal threat, and we need to keep that going and that will be tested.”

Team news from Portman Road to follow shortly.

#2026. West Ham 1-1 Preston: Scott Parker Still Struggling To Unlock Jarrod Bowen

West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division. Whilst we had our chances, it would be a long stretch to suggest we were significantly better than Preston, particularly during a first half in which the visitors created opportunities of their own.

Edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did. In essence, the Hammers lacked magic, and watching our best player pinned to the right flank was depressing.

The statistics certainly make for interesting reading. West Ham registered 30 attempts on goal, but only four were on target. We also hit the woodwork three times, with Bowen and Joël Veltman striking opposite posts during the same passage of play before Edvin Austbø rattled the crossbar shortly after half-time.

Preston took the lead through Liam Lindsay after just 18 minutes, following a corner which Joël Piroe inadvertently flicked towards his own goal.

Konstantinos Mavropanos eventually equalised on the hour mark, heading home Arne Engels’ cross after Manor Solomon had helped create the opening.

Yet even after drawing level, West Ham couldn’t find a winner against a team who arrived at the London Stadium bottom of the Championship.

There were chances, certainly. Tomáš Souček had a late header tipped over, while Mavropanos headed over in stoppage time. But for all the possession and pressure, there was precious little composure in front of goal.

And as far as I’m concerned, this was a match West Ham simply had to win.

What makes the situation particularly frustrating is that we’ve already seen what Bowen can do when he’s given more freedom.

During the remarkable comeback against Cardiff City, our captain was allowed to drift into central positions, where he caused all sorts of problems. His movement, passing and ability to find space helped transform a game which had looked completely lost at half-time.

I was so impressed that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker needed to restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon.

Unfortunately, against Blackburn, Bowen was back operating as a conventional right winger. And against Preston, we saw much the same thing.

That’s not to suggest Bowen didn’t contribute. He was involved throughout and managed eight attempts on goal, including the effort which struck the post.

But there’s a difference between getting Bowen involved in the game and getting the best out of him.

West Ham have spent far too long relying on our captain to produce something special from wide positions, often with defenders able to anticipate where he’s going to receive the ball.

Against Cardiff, we briefly saw something different.

Bowen was the inspiration behind that second-half recovery. He looked far more dangerous when he was able to move into the middle and influence the game rather than remaining tied to the touchline.

I genuinely thought Parker had stumbled upon something which could change West Ham’s season.

Instead, two matches later, we seem to have gone backwards.

Of course, the manager has plenty of other issues demanding his attention.

There were some positives against Preston. Álvarez made his first Championship appearance for West Ham since May 2025 and looked reasonably comfortable in midfield, while young goalkeeper Finlay Herrick produced an excellent double save to prevent the visitors doubling their lead.

Mavropanos also deserves credit for another important goal, particularly given that he is a centre-back who continues to contribute at the other end of the pitch.

But the bigger picture remains deeply concerning.

West Ham simply had to start turning the London Stadium into somewhere opposition teams feared visiting.

Instead, the bottom club have come away with a point, and Parker has now overseen two draws and a defeat in his first three matches.

I appreciate he hasn’t been in the job long, and I’m not suggesting he’s solely responsible for problems which have been developing for some considerable time.

However, the international break gave him an opportunity to work with the players, and I had hoped to see considerably more improvement than we witnessed.

For me, the biggest concern remains our inability to get the best out of Bowen.

We have a player capable of providing the creativity, movement and unpredictability that this team so desperately needs. Yet we’re still asking him to spend most of his time playing in the same predictable areas of the pitch.

West Ham don’t lack effort. Against Preston, they certainly didn’t lack possession or attempts on goal.

And until Scott Parker finds a way of giving Jarrod Bowen the freedom to provide it, I fear we’re going to see plenty more afternoons like this one.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

Too often people talk about statistics but it often detracts from what’s really important in football. The only thing that counts is how many goals you score against what you concede. 79% possession, 30 shots and an expected goals number in excess of 3 mean nothing if you score 1 and so do your opponents. It’s a draw and you both get 1 point, simple really.

I’m not sure I agree on the Bowen argument either. There are 10 other players that we should also expect to perform better at this level. It is a team game after all.

The basic problem I still think we have is that we are too passive and slow all over the pitch. To be unable to beat the bottom team at home is beyond useless if we are serious about promotion. I wish Scott Parker well but I fear this team is no more than a mid table team based on the season so far and more worrying is the fact that there aren’t any obvious characters who have the ability and determination to dig us out of the hole we have created

Agree Bowen contributes more when he is involved in a central forward role.. The main problem is the club lacks decent players. I would suggest that their running stats are one of the lowest in the division. They allow teams to run through them in midfield and don’t press enough

All we ever see is us give ourselves problems then spend the rest of the match chasing the game, against the team that are still bottom, really ?

It’s nowhere near good enough, reality is we’re a mid table Championship team…

#2025. Sergio Navarro’s style and the key individuals: Milan Futuro tactical analysis

Milan Futuro decided to go in a new direction this summer by appointing Sergio Navarro, but is it working so far?

Milan launched the Futuro project ahead of the 2024-25 season. with the aim of creating a pathway for academy players to break into the first team. The project was designed to bridge the physical and technical gap between the Primavera and senior football.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Things didn’t go well in year one, as Daniele Bonera didn’t see out the season as the head coach. He recently stated he didn’t think the squad was ready for the level, and ultimately Massimo Oddo was unable to save the team from relegation to Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football.

With promotion back to Serie C the objective, this summer the Rossoneri turned to Sergio Navarro, a coach with good pedigree in Spain. The Futuro now appear to have a clearer structure, a defined playing identity and the right guidance, as Rohit Rajeev has outlined.

Under Barquero, Milan Futuro operate in a 4-2-3-1 formation. Asanji leads the line, with Ossola playing as the number 10 and Vos and Guernier occupying the wide positions.

Plazotta and Pandolfi form the double pivot, while Cisse and Pagliei partner at centre-back, with Perera and Colombo completing the back four.

Milan Futuro favour a possession-oriented approach, circulating the ball patiently at a measured tempo while waiting for gaps to emerge in the opposition’s defensive structure. They also use passing triangles effectively to create short passing options and play through the opposition’s high press.

In possession, Milan Futuro adopt a 3-1-6 structure, with Barquero showing little hesitation in committing players forward to create numerical overloads in the opposition half.

Asanji positions himself just behind the opposition’s defensive line, keeping the centre-backs occupied and preventing them from stepping forward freely. Meanwhile, Pandolfi and Plazotta maintain parallel positions in the double pivot, providing a stable base for the attacking structure.

In the opposition half, Milan Futuro keep the distances between players very short, allowing them to combine through quick, one-touch passes.

This also helps them create ball-sided overloads, with two or three players surrounding the Milan player in possession to provide close passing options. Once they enter the opposition half, the tempo increases as Milan look to become more direct and progress towards goal.

Similar to Amorim’s approach at Sporting, Milan Futuro form vertical corridors with three players positioned one behind another. This structure facilitates quick passing combinations while also creating movement to manipulate the opposition.

When Milan players drop to form these corridors or create overloads, they often drag defenders with them, opening spaces elsewhere to exploit.

Milan Futuro look to press the opposition high up the pitch, adopting a 4-4-2 shape with a man-oriented pressing scheme. This allows them to put pressure on the opposition’s build-up and restrict the time and space available to play out from the back.

Milan Futuro also set up pressing traps by deliberately leaving the opposition’s wide player unmarked. The pass towards the wide player acts as the pressing trigger, prompting Milan’s players to jump out of their positions and aggressively close down the receiver, while cutting off the available passing options.

Milan Futuro maintain an extremely narrow defensive shape, prioritising the protection of central spaces and forcing the opposition towards the flanks.

Once the opposition attempts to progress through the wide areas, the press shifts across to create numerical overloads around the ball, while Guernier and Colombo provide cover and prevent the opposition from switching play to the opposite flank.

Perhaps the most important aspect of Barquero’s approach is his willingness to build the system around his players’ strengths and allow them the freedom to express themselves.

Rather than focusing solely on tactical adaptability, he appears equally committed to their individual development and helping them grow as footballers. Here are a few examples.

One of Milan Futuro’s methods of chance creation is to play direct passes into Asanji. His ability to position himself between the ball and the opposition defender, using his physicality to shield possession and hold up play, is crucial to this approach.

Rather than asking him to adapt to the role of a more technically oriented, ball-playing striker, Barquero has built a mechanism that makes the most of his existing strengths.

Perhaps the clearest demonstration of Barquero’s coaching ability is his utilisation of Vos and Guernier. Guernier is a natural winger/forward, while Vos is more accustomed to playing as an attacking midfielder.

Within the 3-1-6 structure, Vos often inverts from the left flank into an inside-left role, allowing Perera to provide the width.

At times, he is also given the freedom to interchange positions with Plazotta, allowing him to drop into midfield or advance further up the pitch. This positional freedom helps him develop his midfield qualities and realise his potential.

Guernier, meanwhile, tends to maintain his width, stretching the opposition’s defensive line and creating space for Vos and the other attackers to exploit.

Barquero also gives Guernier the freedom to take on his direct opponent, even when he is outnumbered, allowing him to use his dribbling ability without being restricted by the team’s structure.

Ossola, who is particularly effective at receiving between the lines and turning with the ball, is allowed to operate higher up the pitch, closer to the opposition’s defensive line.

Idrissi, on the other hand, prefers to receive possession deeper, where he can dictate play with his passing range or carry the ball forward through dribbling.

#2017. GdS: Worth the price tag – how Moreira became ‘untouchable’ for Milan and Belgium

It has been a positive international break for Diego Moreira, who continued his excellent form from club football.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport write this morning, Ruben Amorim will welcome Moreira back to Milanello soon. The winger has become a regular starter and producing goals and assists, but the Portuguese coach knows the pitfalls of the match against Frosinone all too well.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Therefore, starting Thursday – when the squad will be fully back together after the day off tomorrow – everyone’s minds will be focused solely on the new busy schedule awaiting the Rossoneri until Christmas. More specifically, seven matches from Sunday until December 19th.

Immediately after the last international break, the Rossoneri drew away to Sassuolo, a result that certainly wasn’t greeted with a smile. The goal is to avoid repeating that misstep against Alvini’s team, and Moreira will be key to that.

Despite his 22 years of age and the €50m valuation plus bonuses that could have weighed heavily on his shoulders, Diego hasn’t taken long to win over Milan fans. In his last six league matches (he missed two due to injury), he’s scored four goals and provided three assists.

He has also demonstrated his ability to switch roles with ease, playing as a winger on the right or left, as a wing-back or even as a full-back. He plays with the boldness of someone who targets his opponent and tries to dribble past him, something that fans always appreciate.

Moreira always seeks one-on-one situations, both due to his strengths and the explicit request of Amorim, who asks his wide players to create numerical superiority. Diego is succeeding remarkably, as his assist for Christian Pulisic in the derby shows, as he got past Carlo Augusto and crossed.

Moreira made the difference against Italy on Sunday too: not only did he score the fourth goal, which he celebrated by making a gesture of ‘one, two, three and four’ with his fingers, but he also kept accelerating, hit the woodwork, shot wide once more and had two shots blocked by his opponents.

He set up De Bruyne for a shot, had more touches than anyone else in the opponents’ area (11) and often took on Calafiori and Dimarco, delighting the crowd with a spectacular backheel. He had around 50 touches and 27/31 completed passes, earning the applause of the entire stadium when he came off.

Moreira is currently captivating thanks to his drive and desire. He’s that way at Milan and he’s that way with the national team. That’s why there’s a version of the Rossoneri with him and another without him which, frankly, isn’t as threatening.

Amorim carefully integrated him into the team’s operations at the start of the season, but now he has broken the padlock off and now considers him a key player in the team. This doesn’t mean he won’t need a breather, given the schedule, but the coach will have to think about the right moments to rest.

With four goals in Serie A (one every 121 minutes), he’s already matched his four goals from last season in Ligue 1, and he has no intention of stopping. He feels the confidence in himself and the team.

The leap from Ligue 1 to Serie A didn’t bother him. In fact, he intends to continue dancing on the pitch, just like in the derby or against Italy. On Sunday, he wants to show he has the same energy with which he brought Italy to its knees. Milan and San Siro await him.

#2009. Duncan Ferguson red carded for first time as manager as unbeaten Glentoran start grinds to halt

Duncan Ferguson was sent off as his unbeaten start as Glentoran manager came grinding to a halt in a 3-2 defeat at Cliftonville in the NIFL Premiership on Friday night.

The former Rangers and Everton striker was shown a straight red card and ordered from the touchline after losing his temper in the aftermath of his side falling behind at Solitude in north Belfast.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Ferguson had angrily protested against Cliftonville's opener believing there was a foul on defender Jarlath O'Rourke in the build-up and was subsequently sent to the stand by referee Ben McMaster.

Ironically, Glentoran had already equalised by the time the card was brandished with Cal Weatherup levelling the match at 1-1 just a minute after Joseph Sheridan had put the hosts in front.

The red card was Ferguson's first as a manager in his 80th appearance in the dugout but the 10th of his career overall after receiving his marching orders on nine occasions during his playing days.

Assistant manager Gary Bollan took charge for the remainder of the game as Glentoran fell behind to a Brian Healy strike in the 67th minute before equalising again through James Douglas with four minutes left.

However, Cliftonville took the three points thanks to a second goal of the night from Sheridan in the 88th minute.

Bollan handled post-match media duties as Ferguson kept his counsel.

"I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul," Bollan said. "It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader. I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a big set of boots to fill."

In the NIFL Premiership, a manager or team official given a red card receives an automatic one-match suspension for the next competitive fixture, with longer bans possible depending on the offence.

It means the former Scotland international will not be in the dugout for the Northern Ireland League Cup match against Larne at The BetMcLean Oval on Tuesday with any further punishment dependent on the content of the referee’s report.

Ferguson had started his Glentoran tenure with two away draws against Coleraine and Carrick before winning his first home game in charge 2-1 against Bangor last Friday. The defeat leaves Glentoran 14 points behind league leaders Linfield.

#2008. Di Marzio: Endrick and Tresoldi deals ‘not a financial issue’ for Milan – the situation

AC Milan have the financial capability to go out and sign their top targets in January, according to Gianluca Di Marzio.

Several reports and even the words of owner Gerry Cardinale have made it very clear that Milan plan to be busy in the winter mercato. The main target seems to be a forward to complete the attack, as well as a centre-back to help out the defensive department too.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Among the names linked have been Real Madrid’s Endrick, Club Brugge’s Nicolo Tresoldi and Sporting CP’s Goncalo Inacio. It’s one thing having the list of names, but it is another having the money and the possibility of doing a deal mid-season with the selling club.

During last night’s segment on Sky, Gianluca Di Marzio (via MilanNews) was asked whether Milan can realistically pursue names like Endrick and Tresoldi, who are likely to cost over €50m each.

“That they has the strength to do these kinds of deals, yes. They demonstrated it over the summer, so I don’t think there’s a financial issue,” he began.

“Whether they manage to sign one of the two… Endrick, as far as we know, José Mourinho hasn’t changed his mind and therefore doesn’t intend to part with him in January. But Endrick is a Cardinale obsession, just as he was a Roma obsession during the summer.

“We’ll have to see if Mourinho changes his mind in the month and a half before the transfer window opens. He hasn’t changed his mind at the moment, so I see the situation as complicated at the moment.

“Just as it’s complicated for Brugge to sell Tresoldi. Brugge are a club that doesn’t need to sell and always sells at least one key player in the summer, precisely to try to get to the end of the season with its players.

“Milan are looking for a striker, looking for a back-up for Ramos. The figures I’ve read, 60-70 million, are very, very high figures to try to convince Brugge to sell him. It’s a deal that – given the player’s objective value – I think is around 50 million. In my opinion.

“But Brugge are unlikely to sell him in January. Above all, Milan is looking for a striker to be a back-up for Ramos; it’s not like Ramos and Tresoldi will play together. In the sense that Milan has always played with a centre-forward.

“Above all, they need to provide this center forward with plenty of playable balls rather than buy another. Because if Ramos doesn’t receive balls in the penalty area, he struggles to score, and Tresoldi struggles to score either.

“They need a striker to get Camarda playing. I think Camarda will go and play and therefore an investment will be needed in a player who can be a suitable deputy for Ramos.”

#2006. Ace bins Motherwell mannequin role after injury setback left him with ‘meaningless’ feeling

Paul McGinn feels ready to make a Motherwell impact after being left like a mannequin through injury.

The 36-year-old centre-back enjoyed a stunning season last term in the Jens Berthel Askou side that finished fourth in the Premiership. He suffered a knee injury away to Rangers towards the end of campaign 25/26 that has limited his involvement with Alfred Johansson’s team this term, making his comeback on Halloween during a 1-0 win versus St Mirren.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He was happy not to botch the clean sheet after appearing as a late sub, but in any case, McGinn is just pleased to be back involved. The club captain loathed his watching brief from the stands that left him feeling useless once the ball got rolling.

McGinn said: "I was content after it finished. I thought, 'imagine if you come on for two minutes and you make a mess of it! I just felt a relief to be back on there and it also helped that we we seen it out. I think the home games you normally as a player have to come, but as captain, you're expected everywhere.

“I was at them all and I don't enjoy it one bit. I feel as if you're just in the way and you're not contributing. I know that everyone knows I can't do anything about it but you just feel like you're a mannequin in the way. I just feel much better even on the bench to know that you can contribute if you're asked to.

"Even if you can be vocal and try and help with tips etc, as soon as the game starts, you're meaningless. So you're just sitting in the stand, people going, when are you back? When are you back? And you are trying not to lie to them, but also telling them nothing. It's just not a nice place to be but it's part of the game."

McGinn will hope to play a role against Rangers at Fir Park on Saturday night as the hosts aim for a huge Premiership win under the lights. The last time Motherwell’s captain faced Ibrox opposition was in the 3-2 win away from home in April, and after a mixed start to Johansson’s tenure domestically, McGinn says they are striving for confidence like they found under predecessor Askou.

He added: “You need a bit of luck in these games as well, of course you do. We won at Ibrox, we should have been out of sight, and then they should have probably been in the lead at one point, then we sneaked one at the end. I've always thought that we need that bit of luck, especially in these games. We had a spell last year where the confidence was so high. It takes you so far in football and it's something we'll be striving to do again.

“If you go on a run then everything becomes easier, how you press, and it's just the nature of being human. We're striving to be in that position again and that's three unbeaten for us. We're striving to be in that position again. I always like the night game. I don't know why, apart from after when you can't sleep until four in the morning! I think it'll be lively out there definitely."

#2004. Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

Sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

“I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”

Gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

“We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

Monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a big opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car company makes sense, despite what I said earlier.

Sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

The Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6

I’m as big a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

“What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton said yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

#1999. Celtic boss addresses midfielder’s ‘deja vu’ return and gives update on duo who were posted missing

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill hopes Luke McCowan’s performance in the 4-1 win over St Mirren can be a catalyst to reignite his Parkhead career.

O’Neill watched his side open up a seven-point gap on second-placed Rangers, who face Motherwell on Saturday evening, blowing away St Mirren before half-time thanks to goals from Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain (33), Camilo Duran (40) and McCowan (42). Callum McGregor (63) added a fourth, with Killian Phillips (69) scoring a consolation penalty for the away side.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Dealt a double blow ahead of the game, midfield pair Benjamin Nygren and Mika Baur both ruled out after picking up injuries on international duty, O’Neill handed McCowan his first start in over two months in the centre of the park alongside Oxlade-Chamberlain.

McCowan has suffered in the last few months, dropping out of the matchday squad after a high-profile error in the defeat to LASK during the Champions League playoffs. Forced to delete his Instagram account to escape personal abuse from sections of the online support, the former Dundee captain had played just 14 minutes since being hauled off at half-time in a 1-0 home defeat to Rangers on September 20.

“I thought he did really well for us,” was O’Neill’s assessment of McCowan’s return to the starting line-up. “It was his first full game for a considerable amount of time. He got the ball once and he played it almost blindly and it was intercepted and I thought ‘oh gosh, here we go’. But he roared back. Took the goal great, and I’m really pleased for him because he’s a really genuine lad.

“It has been tough [for him]. I thought in the game against Rangers, he was thrown into position, and it didn’t start well for him in the match. I thought it felt like deja vu for him after his last game against Rangers at the back end of last season, too. For him today, I felt that was a big boost for him. I’m pleased that there’s a bit of competition for places [in midfield] now. Which is good. But I am pleased that him and Alex got on the field and were able to play. That itself is a confidence booster.”

Duran had the ball in the net for Celtic after five minutes but assistant referee signalled for an offside. The home side thought they’d taken the lead again just after the quarter hour mark, with Duran the disappointed party once more. Blasting home the rebound after Jota’s shot was parried away by Jacob Chapman, the frustrated Colombian looked to sky as the flag went up for offside in the build up for a second time.

A misplaced pass from McCowan signalled a groan from the home crowd as Celtic frustration crept in, however, they needn’t have worried, finding their opener via Oxlade-Chamberlain just after the half-hour mark, with the experienced midfielder slamming home from close range after a positive forward run and cross from Hyun-Jun Yang on the right-wing.

It was no less than the home side deserved, but the momentary VAR check for the opener followed by a blocked goal-bound effort from Killian Phillips offered some unexpected anxiety in the immediate aftermath. O’Neill’s side added further unnecessary stress on a bitterly cold Glasgow afternoon when Yang somehow failed to square to Duran when clean through on goal.

The striker finally got on the scoresheet with a fine side-footed finish from a Kieran Tierney cross shortly before the break.

A moment of redemption followed just 120 seconds later when the returning McCowan collected a neat cut back from Jota in the area to fire home first time beyond Chapman, effectively killing the game before the break.

His first goal since the 5-1 win over Kilmarnock on August 9, a relatively muted celebration followed from McCowan as he was congratulated by his teammates. Virtually out of the picture at Celtic in recent weeks, he’ll hope it’s not his last and that his unexpected reprieve can lead to an extended spell in his boyhood club’s engine room. The victory already wrapped up in nine first-half minutes, McGregor’s placed shot added to the scoreline just after the hour mark, with Phillips’ penalty after a foul from goalkeeper Sam Johnstone on Calvin Ramsay in the box just a consolation.

O’Neill also addressed the omission of Haissem Hassan during his press-match conference and the fitness of Baur and Alistair Johnston. Quashing rumours that the Egyptian was left out against Kilmarnock prior to the international break because he was “unpopular” within the squad earlier this week, the 74-year-old has insisted that both Hassan and Kasper Hogh, who was an unused substitute, will have a part to play against Torreense in the Europa League on Thursday night.

“Kasper will be ready for Thursday,” said O’Neill. “That’s the point. We’re going to need him on Thursday. For want of a better word, it’s more rotation than anything else. Kasper is fine. He’ll [Haissem] will be there for Thursday as well. He’s missed a couple of games. He didn’t come back until Friday from the international break, a couple of them didn’t.

“We were worried about Duran after he travelled halfway around the world, but he was amazing in training.

“Baur is in a boot. If that injury stretches to end of January, we’ll think about making a change [to the Europa League squad]. Alistair was getting a scan and some treatment this weekend in Dublin. We’ll find out about that and get an update. I’m hoping it’s going to be good news. He’s feeling decent within himself now.”

#1998. Dundee United make history as Easter Road empties with Hibs left asking: ‘what has happened?’

Jim Goodwin was full of pride after watching Dundee United make history with a landmark 4-0 demolition of Hibs.

The visitors recorded their biggest ever win at Easter Road, with Zac Sapsford’s first-half double paving the way for a stunning victory before Lyall Cameron and Jesse Randall piled on the misery.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It was a humbling afternoon for Hibs, who thought they had turned a corner under new head coach Marink Reedijk, and the home support deserted the stadium long before the full-time whistle.

Goodwin has experienced some low moments in Leith, losing his job as Aberdeen boss following a 6-0 thrashing to Hibs in January 2023, so was naturally delighted by the margin of this win.

He said: “It’s not been a venue that’s been all too kind to me over the years, so on a personal note I’m very pleased. But, of course, it’s all about Dundee United. I wasn’t aware of that stat but it is something that we can be proud of.

“It’s very rare that you come to a venue like Easter Road against good opposition, especially off the back of their recent results, and have the kind of convincing victory that we’ve just experienced.

“We scored four good goals. Even the build-up for the first, the penalty, was good.”

Sapsford got United off the mark after eight minutes, recovering from having his spot-kick saved by Rafa Sallinger to slot home the rebound after Jason Kerr had fouled him.

The Australian doubled his tally six minutes before half-time, guiding Kevin Ciubotaru’s cross into the net at the near post.

United maintained their momentum after the break, with Cameron firing home off the underside of the bar after Daniel Bennie’s effort had struck the post.

Randall completed the rout, lashing a left-footed shot past Sallinger from 15 yards after being teed up by Tait.

Meanwhile, Hibs head coach Reedijk was left struggling to explain Hibs’ sorry collapse after his side had beaten Hearts in the Premier Sports Cup semi-final and thumped Aberdeen 4-0 before the international break.

The Dutchman said: “What has happened in these two weeks? I haven’t seen these glimpses that it would happen during the week, if you know what I mean.

“And it is not that we didn’t create chances or whatever, it is more this basic behaviour which brings you into matches and continues spells and makes the opponent doubt. We had too many of these moments that didn’t fall our way.

“That is something we need to be very sharp with because we know how nice it is to win, but we also now experience how nice it is not to win and especially in this way. I hate losing but in this way I really hate losing.”

"It's frustrating but we know they're going to start dropping. Once they do, we'll be just fine.

"The forward lads are starting to feel more confident. We just need that to translate to the league games now.

"I don't think it matters who you're playing against, finding the back of the net is massive for your confidence."

Bradford's last league game was October's 3-0 defeat at home to Huddersfield Town.

"When you have two really strong (cup) performances you want to just keep going and take that momentum into the league," said Swan.

"Now it's a chance to get a load of points and win a load of football games.

"It's going to be a tough period. We're going to need the whole team, with how many games there are. You can play Saturday, Tuesday, Saturday and all of a sudden you're nine points ahead of where you were before.

"Over Christmas and New Year, there's going to be a lot of games so there are a lot of chances to push higher up in the table.

"We were in a bit of a good rhythm going into the international break but we've had a good full week of training and we'll use Saturday to hopefully score a few goals and pick that momentum up again."

Bobby Pointon's knee injury puts more emphasis on the other forwards, but Swan says it will inspire them.

"Everyone in the front line will think we've got big shoes to fill there, because he's a class player," he argued. "We'll all do our best to step in and fill that role."

“When you have the confidence of one moment and then you feel the score is getting bigger, you see the players with extra confidence. You see the dynamics there and it’s good they feel it works.

#1994. Rangers avoid title blip as late own goal breaks Motherwell resistance and Celtic kept within eyeline

In the crisp chill of a late November evening in North Lanarkshire, Rangers required a late deflection to prise three vital Scottish Premiership points from the grasp of a resolute and industrious Motherwell side.

With the contest seemingly bound to end 1-1, a potentially significant blip for the visitors in terms of their title aspirations, Ryan Naderi’s 88th-minute effort struck the unfortunate Martin Moormann and looped past goalkeeper Alex Paulsen, inflicting the cruellest of blows on the Steelmen.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

There seemed an almost ritualistic rhythm to Rangers’ recent visits to Fir Park: waves of possession crashing against a disciplined claret-and-amber breakwater, accompanied by the persistent nagging doubt that dominance without ruthlessness invites punishment.

Derek McInnes’s side were living out that exact cautionary tale on their latest visit before Naderi popped up with a crucial late winner.

For the opening 15 minutes, this contest threatened to become a procession. Rangers monopolised the ball and the opening goal arrived after just eight minutes. Motherwell’s defensive structure momentarily frayed under early pressure, allowing centre-back Emmanuel Fernandez to rise unmarked and head home Kim Min-Su’s corner with disarming simplicity.

At that juncture, Motherwell appeared to be unravelling. Within six minutes of falling behind, Alfred Johansson was forced into an early reshuffle when winger Ibrahim Said limped off injured in visible distress to be replaced by Regan Charles-Cook.

Rangers sensed blood. Naderi probed tirelessly, Djeidi Gassama repeatedly cut inside off the left flank to test the Steelmen defence, and Motherwell goalkeeper Alex Paulsen was called upon to produce a string of top-class saves to prevent the visitors from establishing an unassailable cushion.

However, Scottish football rarely rewards aesthetic superiority alone. Having weathered the initial storm without conceding a second, the hosts summoned an equaliser from their first corner of the evening in the 21st minute. Emmanuel Longelo rolled a clever short pass to Tom Sparrow, whose curling delivery into the penalty area found Jake Girdwood-Reich entirely unmarked. The Australian defender needed no second invitation, sweeping a composed finish past Ivor Pandur to restore parity against the run of play.

That subtly altered the psychological temperature inside Fir Park. While Rangers continued to dictate proceedings, racking up nearly 20 attempts on goal, their lack of cutting edge in the final third was glaring. Before the interval, Paulsen defied the visitors once more with a superb reflex stop from Nico Raskin in the 41st minute.

McInnes’ men pressed forward with renewed urgency after a stern half-time team talk. Seven minutes into the second half, Dan Neil drifted into a pocket of space on the edge of the area and drilled a low effort that whistled agonisingly past the post.

Visible frustration began to creep into Rangers’ ranks passing the hour mark as a combination of misplaced passes and poor finishing drew audible groans from the packed away end.

Sensing his team’s grip on the contest loosening, McInnes turned to his bench in the 69th minute, introducing summer signing Kevin Kelsy in place of Gassama to add a greater physical presence in attack alongside Naderi. There was little immediate improvement. Badredine Bouanani raced down the right flank and cut the ball back for Neil, whose shot sailed high and wide.

Motherwell were looking increasingly comfortable and Tawanda Maswanhise tested Pandur from distance as the home side sensed an opportunity to claim something more substantial than a point.

Findlay Curtis was introduced for Rangers and almost made an immediate impact, delivering an excellent cross towards the back post which Naderi was unable to turn home from close range.

Then came another extraordinary intervention from Paulsen. Curtis' effort appeared to have beaten the keeper, who could only palm the ball into the path of Sterling. However, Paulsen recovered magnificently to divert the right-back’s follow-up onto the crossbar. It was a remarkable piece of goalkeeping and, by this stage, it seemed entirely possible that the home side would clinch a share of the spoils.

With two minutes remaining, Rangers finally found the breakthrough their territorial dominance had threatened to deliver. Naderi got his effort away, but Moormann intervened and inadvertently diverted the ball beyond his own goalkeeper. The unfortunate centre-back could do little about the decisive deflection, but the consequences were devastating for Motherwell.

The travelling Rangers support erupted, relief and celebration combining in equal measure. For McInnes, it was a precious late reward for a side that had made unnecessarily hard work of a match they might have settled long before the closing stages.

The victory extends Rangers' unbeaten run in all competitions to 13 matches and ensures they remain in touch with Celtic, moving back within four points of the league leaders with a game in hand.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Grimsby's direction of travel, under Rotherham-born Dave Artell, is upward again following some time in the National League. They are third in League Two.

The Mariners' course hasn't been plain sailing. Their time in the fifth tier provides a bit of a warning to the Millers in the present as they aim to 'bottom out' and start turning their fortunes around.

What the Mariners now have is stability and consistency under Artell. It's a place where Alex Bruce wants to get to.

Bruce said: "Dave's been with Grimsby now for two or three seasons. He's had a chance to build a team and squad.

"They've got some good players and they're sitting where they are in the league for a reason. I came up against them in the play-offs last year with Salford City, so I know quite a lot about them.

"It's easy for me to sit here and say consistency's the way forward and that's what brings success. When you have two or three years in charge of a club and can build your squad and work on things, you get the fruits of that. Dave has done a good job there."

Second-from-bottom Millers are winless in seven league matches, but were buoyed by their recent FA Cup win at League One side Bromley.

Events and game management, as opposed to general performance levels, are what have hurt them of late at league level.

Bruce added: "I know I've taken a little bit of a stick for talking about sending-offs and mistakes and things like that. The positives are, there have been signs of good performances.

"Let's not lose sight of the fact that when we've taken on teams, gone 2-0 up, we were all saying: 'That's more like it.' We've got to build on those moments and build on Bromley. I've got every confidence that my players can be more consistent."

Derek McInnes labelled Ryan Naderi “a big horse” and a textbook example of how to lead the line as a centre-forward after helping Rangers secure a hard-fought 2-1 Premiership victory over Motherwell.

The German striker has been growing in confidence in recent weeks and once again demonstrated his importance to the Ibrox side, combining tireless pressing and intelligent movement which resulted in a scrappy late 88th-minute winner at Fir park.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

McInnes believes Naderi's contribution extends far beyond his goals, insisting his work rate should not overshadow the quality of his all-round performances.

“Ryan’s game is really strong at the minute. He looks like a very confident boy and so he should be,” McInnes said. “Wrongly now, when you think of Ryan or people ask me, it’s about him knocking his pan in. “He looks tired but his performances are always strong. But he gets goals and has an influence. In that system tonight, his was the most important position for us, in terms of running channels and getting hold of the ball. On his side’s performance, McInnes added: “We got our just rewards in the game, absolutely. I thought it was a very good, strong performance and I’ve been told that every one of my outfield players had a shot tonight. I’ve never known a team who practice so much shooting, and crossing and finishing during the week.

“It was the only thing missing for us, I thought it was a top class performance. We mixed the game up well. Our press was strong and we were aggressive. I’m just disappointed it took so long to get the winning goal.”

Deflated Motherwell boss Alfred Johansson admitted his side struggled to cope with Rangers' early intensity, but felt the early loss of Ibrahim Said to injury was a major blow before his side ran out of energy in the closing stages.

“They are title challengers and we have a really tough start to the game,” he said. “They put us down. When we win it back, we give it away again. They get momentum. I don't think it's a free kick that they get before their first goal, but we should defend much, much better on that defensive corner kick.

“In that moment, in the same period, we lose Ibrahim [Said], which is really tough for us, given that the players we have on the bench, many of them in the offensive positions, are not ready to play more than 30 to 45 minutes with high intensity. So it was tough to lose him, and therefore, it's strong of the players to come back and score a goal from a set play and equalise.

“But the last 15-20 minutes, Rangers take completely over and we don't have energy enough in that moment to keep the intensity up.”
